metadata.title: Who Gets the Biggest Raises?
metadata.section: Section C: Labor Dynamics, Wages & Consumer Prices
metadata.data_notes: Uses BLS weekly earnings by percentile (quarterly, full-time workers) instead of the Atlanta Fed tracker, which has no API.

events.label: Recession: pay growth falls to about 1-2%
Low-paid job losses distort the averages

explanation.summary: Do low earners or high earners get bigger raises? This chart compares the yearly change in weekly pay for full-time workers at four points of the pay scale. During the tight job market of 2021-2022, the lowest-paid workers got the fastest raises.
explanation.methodology: Usual weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers from the BLS Current Population Survey: 25th percentile (LEU0252911200), median (LEU0252881500), 75th percentile (LEU0252911300) and 90th percentile (LEU0252911400). Shown as change from the same quarter a year earlier. Quarterly data is filled to monthly. The Atlanta Fed wage tracker has no API, so this BLS series is used instead.

key_findings.title: 2012: Slow Recovery, Flat Pay
key_findings.description: Three years after the recession ended, weekly pay at the 25th percentile was 0.5% lower than a year earlier.
key_findings.significance: Low-wage workers felt the slow recovery longest.

key_findings.title: 2020: A Misleading Jump
key_findings.description: Measured pay growth jumped to about 7-10% for every group. Pay did not really rise this fast; millions of low-paid workers lost their jobs, so the workers who were left had higher average pay.
key_findings.significance: When the mix of workers changes, averages can mislead.

key_findings.title: 2021-2022: Low Earners Lead
key_findings.description: In December 2021 the 25th percentile's pay was up 7.5% against 3.2% for the top 10%. By June 2022 it was 9.2% against 6.7%.
key_findings.significance: A shortage of workers gave the lowest-paid the most bargaining power.
